paragraphs.heading: Bouncing back
paragraphs.text: Reflection happens when a wave meets the boundary between two different materials and turns back into the material it came from. Light, sound and water waves all do it. In sound, reflection gives us echoes and makes sonar work. Geologists rely on it when they study seismic waves.

paragraphs.heading: The law of reflection
paragraphs.text: At a mirror-like surface, a wave leaves at the same angle it arrived at. To measure those angles, imagine a line standing straight out from the surface at the point where the ray hits; this line is called the normal. The law then says θᵢ = θ_r: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The incoming ray, the outgoing ray and the normal all sit in one flat plane, with the two rays on opposite sides of the normal.

paragraphs.heading: Mirror-like or scattered
paragraphs.text: Reflected light can be specular, meaning mirror-like, or diffuse, where the energy comes back but the image is lost. Which one you get depends on the kind of surface. A typical mirror is a sheet of glass with a metal coating, and the coating does most of the reflecting. Clear materials such as water and glass reflect too, but usually less well than a mirror.

paragraphs.heading: Images in mirrors
paragraphs.text: Specular reflection makes images. A flat mirror gives a mirror image that seems swapped left to right, because we judge it against how we would look if we were turned around to stand where the image is. A curved mirror can make an image larger or smaller, and such mirrors may be spherical or parabolic in shape.

paragraphs.heading: Part reflected, part passed on
paragraphs.text: Light can reflect any time it crosses from one material into another with a different refractive index. Usually some of the light reflects at the boundary and the rest carries on and bends, which is called refraction. Equations called the Fresnel equations predict how the light splits between the two. When light reflects off a material with a higher refractive index than the one it is in, its wave is flipped by 180°, an effect that matters in thin-film optics.

paragraphs.heading: Why materials reflect
paragraphs.text: In classical physics, light is an electromagnetic wave. When it hits a material, it makes the atoms, or the electrons in a metal, jiggle slightly, and each one sends out a small wave of its own in every direction. These little waves add up to produce both reflection and refraction. In glass, the reflected light is the sum of the backward-going waves from all the electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Reflecting X-rays
paragraphs.text: Reflection is not limited to visible light. Radio waves of VHF and higher frequencies reflect, which matters for radio and radar. Special grazing mirrors can bounce even hard X-rays and gamma rays, as long as the rays come in at a shallow angle. X-ray telescopes use a narrowing tunnel whose walls send the rays at low angles toward a detector at the focus, because an ordinary mirror would just let the X-rays pass through.
